records.request:
PR title: feat(runtime): typed provider-capacity start refusal (EX_TEMPFAIL)

PR description:
## Summary

When a start is refused by the endpoint it launches against (broker pool full, tunnel down), Gas City treats it as a session-specific crash. The manager's stale-key recovery then fires on every such refusal. It clears `session_key`, `started_config_hash` and the priming markers, arms a continuation reset, and **launches again** into the same full endpoint. So every refused start costs two launches, and a session with a conversation loses its resume handle to capacity pressure.

Measured on one production city (maintainer-city) over 7 days: 94.8% of enqueued starts failed, and 99.97% of those failures carried `fresh start after stale key:`, meaning two launches per attempt.

This PR adds a typed capacity refusal at the process boundary and stops the manager from retrying a refusal fresh.

## The exit-75 contract

A launched agent command (or its launcher) that exits with **75** (`EX_TEMPFAIL`, sysexits.h: "temporary failure; retry later") **during startup** declares that the endpoint it needs is at capacity or temporarily unavailable. That is retryable and not the session's fault. Any other exit stays session-specific, as today. Pane text is never consulted. This is the same convention gate commands already use (`convergence.GateInfraExitCode`).

The Manifold native launchers adopt this contract in gascity/manifold#479. The existing tunnel-down check already exits 75.

- `runtime.ExitCodeTempFail`, `runtime.ErrProviderCapacity`, `*runtime.CapacityError`, `runtime.IsProviderCapacity`.
- `CapacityError` matches **both** `ErrProviderCapacity` and the provider's original error under `errors.Is` (so it is still `ErrSessionDiedDuringStartup` for tmux). Its message is exactly the original's.

## Producers

| Provider | How 75 is observed |
|---|---|
| tmux | When the pane is found dead during the startup readiness/liveness steps, `startupDeadSessionError` reads `#{pane_dead_status}`/`#{pane_dead_signal}` **once**. The same values go into `start-stderr.log`. Status `75` with no signal → `CapacityError`. It is not `ErrServerDegraded`, so the token-fenced teardown still runs. |
| exec | New pure `classifyExecExit`. A `start` op exit 75 → `CapacityError`, and the box is still torn down. A name collision still wins, keeping `ErrSessionExists` and skipping teardown. On other ops, 75 is an ordinary failure. Documented in `docs/reference/exec-session-provider.md`. |
| acp | The exit status is no longer discarded. After a failed handshake, Start waits for the monitor to reap the agent and reads `ProcessState.ExitCode()`; 75 → `CapacityError`. Start's own SIGKILL yields a signal (`-1`), so a 75 is always the agent's own choice. |
| auto / hybrid / worker handle | Pass the error through via `%w`. |

**Not classified (unchanged behavior):**
- subprocess, ssh and k8s: none of them exposes a start exit status;
- a tmux death after `Start` returns nil (the post-start stale-key check);
- a tmux launcher that exits before remain-on-exit is set, which leaves no pane to read.

## Session manager

In `ensureRunning` and `ensureRunningRuntimeOnly`, a capacity refusal skips `retryFreshStartAfterStaleKey`. The result is one launch, no resume-metadata clear and no continuation reset. The ACP route is released and the typed error is returned. All other startup deaths keep the existing recovery (SESSION-START-009).

## What this does not change yet

cmd/gc does not consume the new type. A refused **reconciler** start still goes through today's `commitStartFailure` accounting: pending-create rollback, the startup-health episode, and `recordWakeFailure`, which can still apply the conversation reset unless the transcript probe finds the conversation. SESSION-START-013 is scoped to the manager. A follow-up PR adds a per-endpoint capacity breaker on the legacy start path: gated wakes, one half-open probe, and a capacity commit arm with no rollback or accrual.

## Tests

| Test | Mutation it catches (each verified failing on a `git archive` copy) |
|---|---|
| `TestCapacityError_MatchesSentinelAndCausePreservesMessage` | `Unwrap` returning only the sentinel; a suffix on `Error()` |
| `TestStartupDeadSessionError_ExitTempFailIsCapacity` | wrong code compared; classification dropped; pane status read twice |
| `TestStartupDeadSessionError_BrokerTextWithExitOneIsNotCapacity` | pane-text ("HTTP 503") matching |
| `TestStartupDeadSessionError_SignalOrMissingStatusIsNotCapacity` | missing status or a (numeric) signal treated as capacity |
| `TestCapacityErrorIsNotServerDegraded` | a classification that would skip the fenced teardown |
| `TestClassifyExecExit_TempFailOnlyForStartOp` | 75 mapped to nil like 2; 75 applied to every op |
| `TestClassifyExecExit_CollisionBeatsTempFail` | collision and capacity arms swapped |
| `TestStart_Exit75TearsDownBoxAndReturnsCapacity` | teardown skipped for capacity |
| `TestACPHandshakeStartError_ProcessExitTempFailIsCapacity` | classification dropped; any nonzero/-1 exit treated as capacity |
| `TestEnsureRunningRuntimeOnly_CapacityRefusalSkipsFreshRetryAndKeepsKey` | guard removed; only `ensureRunning` fixed; guard after `clearStaleResumeMetadata` |
| `TestEnsureRunning_CapacityRefusalSkipsFreshRetryAndKeepsKey` | only `ensureRunningRuntimeOnly` fixed |
| `TestEnsureRunningRuntimeOnly_PlainStartupDeathStillRetriesFresh` | guard too broad (non-capacity deaths lose the recovery) |

Per TESTING.md, there are no new sleeps or listeners, and no new tests call ACP or subprocess `Start`. The ACP helper is pure over the exit code, because a real `ProcessState` would add a subprocess to the Small-test resource ledger. That leaves one gap: removing the one-line `cmd.ProcessState.ExitCode()` wiring inside ACP `Start` cannot be caught without an ACP `Start` test. PR title: Fix proxy-process readiness window after helper spawn

PR description:
## What this changes

A proxy-process service can be marked degraded during a controller tick even when its replacement helper is healthy. The readiness deadline previously started before the orphan-process scan and was shared by services started later in the same tick. Under load, those steps could consume most or all of the five-second window before a helper existed.

The readiness window now starts immediately after each helper is spawned. The production limit remains five seconds; each new helper receives that full window. A regression test crashes a helper, supplies a stale tick time, and verifies the replacement becomes ready.

## Review notes

- The readiness timeout becomes a package variable so tests can use a longer bound on a loaded host. The test package sets it once during initialization and has no parallel tests; production retains the five-second value.
- No configuration, API, or migration changes.

PR title: fix(test): never hand the operator's HOME to a bd or dolt a test forks

PR description:
v1.5.0 release blocker (test isolation; main only, no backport).

## Problem

On 2026-09-29 at 14:55:49Z, an acceptance test binary started `/tmp/gc-acceptance-3929333879/bin/dolt sql-server --config /home/ubuntu/.beads/shared-server/dolt-server-config.yaml`. That config belongs to the operator's own bd shared server, because their `~/.beads/config.yaml` sets `dolt.shared-server: true`. One second later the same run rewrote `~/.beads/config.yaml`. The shared server it started was later left running from a deleted temp binary, and a live bd workspace was bound to its port.

## Root cause

`test/acceptance/helpers/env.go:43` (`NewEnv`) keeps the real `HOME` on purpose. The platform supervisor refuses an overridden HOME (`platformSupervisorHomeOverrideError`), so gc isolates through `GC_HOME` instead. Every bd the harness ran inherited that HOME:

- **The culprit:** `ProvisionBeadsDatabase` runs `bd init --server --server-host … --server-port …` with `env.List()` (`test/acceptance/helpers/beads_topology.go:317-322`). In shared-server mode, bd ignores the explicit host and port and starts the host-wide server under `~/.beads/shared-server`, using the first `dolt` on PATH. For a topology run that is `<TempDir gc-acceptance-*>/bin/dolt`, the `TopologyEnv` link dir, which matches the incident's binary path exactly. Reproduced with a canary HOME: bd called `dolt config --global` against the canary and created `canary/.beads/shared-server`.
- **Same exposure:**
  - the TestMain `bd migrate schema` probe (`bd_schema_parity.go:94`) dials the shared server and writes `~/.beads/machine-id` and `~/.config/bd`;
  - gc-forked bd in every bd-backed acceptance suite;
  - the `os.Environ()` passthroughs in `beads_cli_contract_test.go` and `tier_b/pool_workquery_test.go`;
  - integration's real bd, where `pinRealHomeEnv` applies and the file-store shim forwards `os.Environ()`;
  - the conditional-writer integration runner in `internal/beads`.

## Fix

gc keeps the real HOME, and the supervisor guard is unchanged. bd and dolt get their own home instead, through a new shared test helper, `test/toolhome`:

- **`Environ`:** points HOME and the XDG base dirs at a test-owned home, drops `BEADS_*`/`BD_*` except names the caller keeps, and pins `BD_DOLT_SHARED_SERVER=false` (the viper env binding that outranks every config layer) and `BD_DISABLE_METRICS=1` (a fresh home would otherwise print bd's first-run metrics notice into parsed output). The home must exist: bd v1.0.4 panics on a HOME it cannot stat, so every caller creates it.
- **`WrapperScript`:** a POSIX `bd` that does the same and then execs the real bd. It is used where gc resolves bd itself, via PATH or `BD_BIN`. HOME is always replaced. XDG vars and the pinned `BD_*` switches get defaults only when the caller left them unset, so a deliberately seeded layer still reaches bd.
- **Acceptance:**
  - every `Env` gets a tool home;
  - `NewEnv` stages the configured bd behind the wrapper ahead of the host PATH, and so do `TopologyEnv`, `proxiedEnv` (plus the recording-BD chain), worker inference (`BD_BIN`) and the tutorial goldens;
  - direct bd/dolt forks use `Env.ToolList()` or `ToolCommand`;
  - the schema probe and `ProvisionBeadsDatabase` run re-homed.
- **Integration:** TestMain removes the host's XDG/`BEADS_*`/`BD_*` from the process, and `realBDBinary` becomes the wrapper. The file-store shim and every direct real-bd call already go through `realBDBinary`.
- **`internal/beads`:** the conditional integration runner runs bd with an exact, re-homed env.
- **F9 shared-server test:** now opts back into the user-level layer explicitly (`BD_DOLT_SHARED_SERVER=""` plus its seeded `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`), so it still tests what it did before.

## Tests

The guard tests are in `test/acceptance/helpers/tool_home_test.go`. They are untagged, so they run in the unit shards. Each one:

1. points HOME, the XDG dirs, `BEADS_DOLT_SHARED_SERVER=1`, `BD_DOLT_SHARED_SERVER=true`, `BEADS_DIR` and `BEADS_SHARED_SERVER_DIR` at a canary home whose bd configs say `shared-server: true`;
2. drives one harness path: the schema probe, `ProvisionBeadsDatabase`, a topology PATH bd, the Env PATH bd, or an explicit-layer opt-in;
3. requires that no bd child's environment names the canary, and that the canary is byte-for-byte unchanged (mode, size, mtime and hash of every entry).

A real-bd variant runs the exact `bd init --server` with a recording `dolt` stub that refuses to start. `test/toolhome` has unit tests for `Environ`, the wrapper (run through a stub) and the process scrub. Integration adds `TestIntegrationRealBdIsTheToolHomeWrapper` and `TestIntegrationEnvCarriesNoHostBdState`.

The real-bd test reported "bd ran dolt against the host home", "bd created the host's shared-server root" and "the host home was modified". PR title: feat(api): add POST /session/{id}/reset

PR description:
## Summary

`gc session reset` is CLI-only today (`cmd/gc/cmd_session_reset.go` -> `worker.Handle.Reset` -> `Manager.RequestFreshRestart`, then a controller poke). API-only clients (the dashboard, scripted clients, ACP front ends) have no way to start a fresh provider conversation on an existing session.

This PR adds `POST /v0/city/{cityName}/session/{id}/reset`:

- Resolves the session with `resolveSessionIDWithConfig` (aliases and named sessions work the same as other session commands).
- Calls `workerHandleForSession(...).Reset(ctx)`, so it goes through the worker boundary and records the existing `worker.operation` reset event, then pokes the controller. The controller restarts the session on the next continuation epoch, so the provider starts a new conversation. The bead is kept.
- Returns `200 {status: "ok", id}`. An unknown session returns 404. A closed session returns 409, and nothing is written or poked. The request needs the usual `X-GC-Request` CSRF header.
- The operation is classified as an action on an existing resource in the idempotency guard (`exemptFromIdempotency`), the same as stop/kill/suspend/wake.

**Parity note:** at the bead level this matches `gc session reset` (`restart_requested` + `continuation_reset_pending`). Unlike the CLI, the endpoint does **not** clear a tripped named-session respawn circuit breaker, because that state sits behind the controller socket. The operation description says so. That is left as a follow-up.

Generated artifacts regenerated: OpenAPI spec (`internal/api/openapi.json`, `docs/reference/schema/openapi.*`), Go genclient, dashboard TS client, embedded dashboard `dist/`, and the Bazel BUILD files.

Stack: independent (based on `main`). Part of the ACP-support PR set (related: #6541, #6543, #6544, #6552). It does not depend on any of them.

- [x] New handler tests (written first; they failed with 404 before the route existed): `internal/api/handler_session_reset_test.go` covers the fresh-restart metadata, the controller poke, the `worker.operation` reset event, 404 for an unknown session, 409 for a closed session with no side effects, and 403 without the CSRF header

PR description:
## Problem
RC Gate run 36621609134 (release/v1.5.0 @ e0cb0c5e4f), job Mac regression / Mac / integration packages / core: `TestBackupOrderTakesOverALegacyBackupDestination` fails with `bd's default destination is not at the legacy artifact URL`. `dolt_backups` ends up holding both `default,file:///private/var/folders/...` and `legacydb-backup,file:///var/folders/...`.

The problem is in the test fixture, not the product. On macOS, `t.TempDir()` is under `/var`, which is a symlink to `/private/var`.
- `mol-dog-backup.sh:21` canonicalises the city with `pwd -P`.
- Dolt's backup address-conflict check compares URL strings.

bd's `resolveDoltBackupURL` is identical in v1.3.0 and v1.3.1-rc.2, so this has nothing to do with the bd pin. The test arrived with the proxreaper backport and had never run on Mac before.

Register the legacy entry at the `filepath.EvalSymlinks`'d city path, which is where a real legacy order would have put it. Test-only change.

Reproduced on Linux with `TMPDIR` pointed at a symlink and the released bd v1.3.1-rc.2:

PR title: perf(orders): move order dispatch off the controller tick onto its own lane

PR description:
## Summary

Move order dispatch off the controller tick onto its own lane.

**Why:** on maintainer-city, `dispatch_orders` takes about 32s of a ~120s controller tick, and the controller goroutine is 97–100% busy in ticks. Everything queued behind the tick waited on order gates: reload replies, pokes, convergence, and every session action. A due order in turn waited behind every session phase. This is a latency and structure change under the legacy reconciler; what dispatch does is unchanged.

## Behavior changes

- Order dispatch runs on its own goroutine, not in the tick. Each tick wakes the lane instead of dispatching, so a due order never waits behind session reconciliation and the tick never waits on order gates.
- A wake runs a pass at once if the lane has been idle at least as long as its last pass ran, and otherwise as soon as it has. While a pass fits in the patrol interval the lane is busy at most half the time (a longer pass is followed by one interval idle). It never runs two passes back to back, and cities with short passes keep main's poke latency.
- A timer reset after every pass runs a pass one patrol interval after the last one ended if nothing else has: the backstop for a wedged tick. On maintainer-city (32s pass against a 15s patrol interval) the backstop always comes first, so the rate is one pass per interval plus pass time.
- Reloads never wait on a pass. A generation guard, read with the pass's config as one pair, stops a stale rescan from overwriting a reload's dispatcher. A forced shutdown that overlaps a running pass skips the order drain.
- The lane has its own FS-pressure skip/force count, separate from the tick's. Each tick that wakes the lane records the age of the lane's last pass that reached dispatch, so a lane that is stuck or starved by pressure shows up in the trace.

## Design

- **Lane** (`cmd/gc/orders_lane.go`): same shape as the route-recovery and completions lanes. It has its own goroutine, `safeTick` recovery per pass (#663), and a context that `run()` cancels and joins on every exit. It starts right after the synchronous startup-orders pass, so MAINT-008 still dispatches before the cold-start reconcile and orders keep firing during it. Each pass runs the FS-pressure gate, the managed-Dolt preflight (now serialized, since three paths run it), the periodic rescan, install of any staged dispatcher, the tracking/nudge-mail watchdogs, and `dispatch()`. A pass is its own `orders` trace cycle; `dispatch_orders` keeps its site and name.
- **Duty-cycle pacing:** a small pure helper (`ordersLanePace.wakeWait`) computes how long a wake must wait: until idle ≥ the last pass's duration, capped at the backstop. Wakes that arrive during the wait, including mid-pass, join one pass.
- **Backstop:** one timer, reset at the end of every pass, fires one patrol interval after the last pass ended. There is no new config knob.
- **Generation pair:** a reload publishes its config and then, when it stages a dispatcher, bumps an order-set generation under the lane's `setMu`. Each pass reads the generation and the one config snapshot the whole pass uses (trace, rescan, watchdogs) as a pair under that lock. The rescan stages only if the generation is unchanged. Nothing a pass runs reads `cr.cfg` directly.
- **Reloads:** a reload stages the rebuilt dispatcher and installs it immediately if the lane is idle (the old synchronous behavior). Otherwise the next pass installs it, draining the outgoing dispatcher first. A pass already in flight finishes on the outgoing dispatcher. Reply latency stays independent of order count (#3206).
- **Shutdown:** a normal shutdown runs after `run()` has joined the lane, so it drains with the lock free. A forced shutdown that overlaps a running pass logs `orders lane still running; skipping order dispatcher drain` and skips the drain rather than block on the pass or race it. A pass rechecks the context after taking the pass lock.
- `max_dispatches_per_tick` keeps its name; its description now says the budget is per lane pass (docs and schema regenerated). Architecture docs (`orders.md`, `controller.md`, `health-patrol.md`) describe the lane rather than a dispatch tick phase.

## Tests

New tests use `testing/synctest` virtual time for pacing, and the package hang budget (`awaitClose`/`awaitCond`) elsewhere. No new `time.Sleep` or listeners. Each new test was checked against a mutation on a `git archive` copy:

| Test | Mutation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `TestOrdersLaneTimerIsOnlyABackstop` | backstop timer swapped for a free-running `time.NewTicker` | FAIL (`timer=1`, want 0) |
| (i) `TestOrdersLaneWakeAfterShortPassRunsAfterItsDutyGap` | wake ignored (waits for backstop) / wake runs immediately regardless | FAIL / FAIL |
| (ii) `TestOrdersLaneWakeAfterLongPassWaitsForGapOrBackstop` | wake ignored / immediate / wait not capped at the backstop | FAIL / FAIL / FAIL |
| (iii) `TestOrdersLaneMidPassWakeNeverRunsBackToBack` | wake ignored / immediate | FAIL / FAIL |
| `TestOrdersLaneForcesPassUnderPressureDespiteTickForces` | tick's FS episode reset also clears the lane's counters | FAIL (no lane dispatch in 6 passes) |
| `TestOrdersLanePressureSkippedPassIsNotALastPass` | `notePass` deferred at pass start | FAIL |
| `TestOrdersLanePassConfigIsNeverReadBeforeGeneration` | config snapshot read before the generation / generation read outside the lock | FAIL / FAIL |
| `TestOrdersLaneForcedShutdownSkipsDrainWhileLaneHoldsPass` | shutdown `TryLock` → `Lock` | FAIL (hang budget) |
| `TestOrdersLaneDispatchesDuringColdStartReconcile` | `startOrdersLane` moved after the startup reconcile | FAIL (hang budget) |

Also covered: a stale rescan racing a reload, a real reload vs a concurrent lane (race detector), reload-during-pass non-blocking install, panic recovery, FS-pressure skip/force on the lane, and the tick trace's last-pass fields.

records.title: fix(beads): stop large graph cooks failing with SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT (517)
records.request:
PR title: fix(beads): stop large graph cooks failing with SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT (517)

PR description:
## Summary

Large workflow cooks into the SQLite graph store fail under controller load with

```
instantiating formula "mol-adopt-pr-v2" on bd-…: clearing claim fence for "gcg--9223372036854765162": database is locked (517)
```

On maintainer-city (1.4 GB graph, about 1 foreign commit/s, load average 80–135) every cook of one `mc-5495l` workflow failed across 20 attempts. Other sources needed up to 20 restarts. WAL checkpoint, ANALYZE and VACUUM did not help.

## Root cause

All three defects are in `internal/beads/sqlite_store.go` and `sqlite_store_graph_apply.go`, and they compound.

1. **The id allocator overflows int64.**
   - The graph holds `gcg-9223372036854775806`.
   - `numericIDSuffix` reads the `-N` of an overflowed id as positive `N`. It also discards `strconv.Atoi`'s range error, which clamps an overlong suffix to `MaxInt64`.
   - As a result, `recoverSequence` and `reseedSeqFromTx` seed the sequence next to `MaxInt64`. `nextID`'s atomic `Add` then wraps to `MinInt64`.
   - Every cook then walks the fully occupied `gcg--9223…` block one `idExistsTx` at a time. On the live city that is 10,647 ids, and it grows by one per successful cook. A read-only walk from `MinInt64` predicted the exact id a failed attempt died on.
   - `ensureSequenceAtLeast` used a signed compare, so each node's reseed dragged the sequence back to `MaxInt64` and the next node walked the block again.
2. **The transaction is deferred.**
   - `ApplyGraphPlan` does all the minting reads before its first write (`clearClaimFenceTx`), so the first read pins a WAL snapshot.
   - Any controller commit during the walk makes the read->write upgrade fail with `SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT` (517). `busy_timeout` cannot wait that out.
3. **The retry is too weak.** `retryOnBusy` makes 3 retries at a flat 150 ms, and each retry redoes the walk.

## Fix

- **Overflow-safe allocator.**
  - Sequence values are bounded by `sqliteSequenceCeiling` (`1<<62`).
  - Own-prefix ids parse as signed int64, and only values in `(0, ceiling]` count toward recovery, reseed, pinned-id lifts and floors. Near-`MaxInt64` and negative ids are ignored: the allocator can never mint them, so they cannot collide.
  - Reaching the ceiling is an explicit `sequence exhausted` error. The allocator never wraps.
- **Bounded collision handling.**
  - `mintUniqueIDTx` steps over at most 64 occupied ids with indexed point lookups before doing one whole-table reseed.
  - After the reseed the next id is guaranteed free, because the write lock is held. So a stale floor costs a bounded amount instead of a walk.
- **`BEGIN IMMEDIATE` on the write connection** (`_txlock=immediate` on a writer-only DSN).
  - The write lock is taken before the first read, where `busy_timeout` does wait, so a snapshot cannot go stale mid-transaction.
  - This covers every read-modify-write transaction on the store, not just graph apply.
  - The read pool and the read-only/private-recovery DSNs stay deferred.
- **Busy backoff.** Jittered exponential backoff: 6 retries starting at 100 ms and doubling, capped at 2 s, so at most 5.1 s of sleep. The sleeper is injectable for tests.
- **`gc workflow delete-source` slowness** (a 189 s dry run that returned `already_clean`).
  - Metadata-filtered `List` (`ListByMetadata`, the source lookups) used to walk every main-tier row. Without `sqlite_stat1` (the exact-schema preflight forbids `ANALYZE`), the planner drove it off `idx_beads_tier_status (tier=?)` and fetched every main-tier row to test `id IN (metadata subquery)`.
  - With a metadata filter present, `tier`, `status`, `type` and `assignee` are now residual (`+b.tier='main'`), and the query drives off `idx_metadata_key_value` -> primary key.

records.request:
PR title: fix(doctor): never start a stopped proxied store

PR description:
v1.5.0 rc1 fix: `gc doctor` must never start servers.

## Problem
On a stopped bd-owned proxied city, a full `gc doctor` (and `gc doctor --fix`) starts the proxy (`bd db-proxy-child --idle-timeout -1ns`) and a `dolt sql-server`. They never exit, because gc-owned scopes run with idle timeout "never", and `BEADS_DOLT_AUTO_START` does not apply on the proxied path (F7). This is pre-existing on release/v1.5.0 with both bd v1.3.0 and the 1.3.1 hotfix (see the delta section of review-nestedcfg.md for #6814).

## Root cause
Nothing in `buildDoctorChecks` (`cmd/gc/cmd_doctor.go`) asked whether the store was running before reading it. The reads happen in this order:
1. `newSessionProvider()`, behind agent-sessions, zombie-sessions and orphan-sessions, reads the city store while the checks are being registered (`bd list --label=gc:session`), which wakes it.
2. The bead-store preflight (`list --limit 1`) then finds the store reachable, so `storeOK` is true.
3. About 20 store-reading checks follow (routed-to, backlog, order-firing-current, custom-types, hold-label, and others), roughly 108 bd calls.

## Fix
- `doctor.ProxiedStoreNotRunning(scopeRoot)` asks gc's own endpoint inspection whether a proxied scope's proxy is running. That is `proxyendpoint.Inspect` over the proxy record and the process table: no bd call, no dial. It is the same gate proxied-backup-coverage uses since #6814.
- `cmd/gc/doctor_store_gate.go` caches the answer per scope for one doctor run and applies it before any store read:
  - **Stopped city:**
    - These checks keep their names but report `not checked: store not running` (StatusOK on a stopped city, a warning if the controller is up; no fix): the three session checks (the session provider is never built), every check the preflight gates, order-firing-current, custom-types:city and hold-label-conventions:city.
    - The preflight itself is not run.
    - The skill-sink check skips its live-session sinks; its static sinks still scan.
  - **Stopped rig:** its beads, custom-types and hold-label checks do the same. The shared store factory and the order-history lookup refuse the rig, so city-level checks that walk rigs report it as "skipped: ... not checked: store not running" instead of waking it.
- `gc doctor --fix`: the stand-ins have no fix, and every fix that needs a stopped store belongs to a replaced check, so `--fix` cannot start a store either.
- Checks that don't read the store run unchanged: config, dolt files and sizes, backup files, proxied endpoint and idle-timeout, shared-server, worktrees and pack scripts. A running city is unchanged, and the check name set is unchanged (golden test).
- `engdocs/design/beads-proxied-local-default.md` documents the rule.
- **Running city, dead proxy:** when the controller is up, the not-running stand-ins report a **warning** with a fix hint, so a real fault isn't hidden. They report OK only for a stopped city.
- `TestProxiedNativeLifecycle` (reviewer's rework) now drives the lane's admission through `gc status --json` and counts bd calls, then reads the payload through doctor once the proxy is live. There is no escape hatch.

## Tests
- **Acceptance** `TestDoctorLeavesAStoppedProxiedCityStopped` (`acceptance_a`): a real M1 proxied city plus a rig, stopped with 0 processes.
  - Full `gc doctor --json`, then `gc doctor --fix --json`: 0 proxy/Dolt processes after each. agent-sessions, beads-store, custom-types:city and custom-types:<rig> are reported as not checked.
  - Passes with bd v1.3.0 (CI's pin) and with the hotfix bd 0cba03281c, so no skip is needed.
  - With the gate disabled it fails: `gc doctor started 4 process(es)` (two proxies, two Dolts).
- **Unit (cmd/gc):**
  - `TestBuildDoctorChecksNeverReadsAStoppedCityStore`: every city and rig store check is not-checked and has no fix; the preflight is not run.
  - `TestBuildDoctorChecksNeverReadsAStoppedRigStore`: city checks run; rig checks are not-checked; the factory refuses the rig.
  - Updated `TestBuildDoctorChecksProxiedBackupCoverageNeverWakesAStore` to model a running proxy whose preflight fails.
- **Unit (doctor):** `TestProxiedStoreNotRunningOnlyForAStoppedProxiedScope`, `TestStoreNotRunningCheckKeepsTheNameAndHasNoFix`.

- `TestProxiedNativeLifecycle`: all 8 rows pass locally with bd v1.3.0.
- `TestBuildDoctorChecksWarnsOnAStoppedStoreUnderARunningCity`, `TestStoreNotRunningCheckWarnsWhenTheCityIsRunning`.

## Risks
- A proxied scope whose proxy record is unreadable, or belongs to someone else, reads as "not running", so its store checks are skipped rather than run. That errs toward never starting a server.
- Direct, doltlite and external non-proxied scopes are never gated: their stores don't start on a read.
- `doctor.StoreNotRunningCheck` reports StatusOK. A stopped city is healthy, and doctor's exit code doesn't change.

Refs: review-nestedcfg.md (delta, section 2), F7. v1.5.0 rc1 blocker.

PR title: feat(acp): reap orphaned ACP runtimes by GC_SESSION_ID

PR description:
## Summary

The ACP provider does not implement `runtime.ProcessTableScanner`, so `Manager.killExistingOrphans` never reaps ACP agents that outlive their supervisor. It also misses agent tool children that left the agent's process group and were reparented to init. Separately, the `auto` router doesn't forward the scanner at all. In any city that mixes tmux/subprocess sessions with ACP sessions, orphan reaping was therefore off for **every** session, including the tmux and subprocess ones.

- **`internal/runtime/acp/proctable.go`**: `FindRuntimesBySessionID` calls `proctable.ScanBySessionID` and decides tracking from **positive owner liveness**, not only this process's connections:
  - `Start` sets `GC_ACP_CONTROL_SOCKET` (the absolute control-socket path) in every agent's environment; tool children and daemons inherit it.
  - A root is tracked when (1) this Provider holds a live conn for its `GC_SESSION_ID` (with `ProviderName`), or (2) its marker names a socket this Provider created for a session still in its startup handshake, or (3) its marker names a socket owned by another gc process and that socket accepts a connection.
  - The owner's listener closes when the agent process exits and dies with the owner. So a crashed agent (even while its dead conn is still in the table), a supervisor-restart survivor, and their escaped tool children are all untracked and get reaped.
  - This closes a reviewer-found hazard: without the marker, a gc process that does not own a session (a CLI `gc session nudge`/`attach` next to the controller, possibly with a different ACP state dir) saw the controller's live agent as untracked and its pre-start orphan kill could terminate it whenever its own `IsRunning` check missed the socket.
  - Roots without a marker are tracked only by this Provider's live conns. If the marker can't be read, the root is kept and the error is surfaced.
  - `TerminateRuntime` refuses `PID <= 1` and otherwise calls the identity-checked `proctable.KillByPID` (SIGTERM, then SIGKILL, bound to the process start time). The seam-backed provider (`cutover.go`) passes both methods through.
- **`internal/runtime/proctable/environ_*.go`** (new files): `ProcessEnvValue(pid, key)` reads one variable from a process's environment, using the same scan root and the same #2839 live-`/proc` test guard as `ScanBySessionID` (darwin via `ps eww`).
- **`internal/runtime/auto/proctable.go`**: `auto.Provider` implements `ProcessTableScanner`:
  - It scans every backend that can scan and merges the results by PID. A root counts as tracked if any backend tracks it, and the tracking backend's `ProviderName` is kept.
  - Each backend's errors are labeled and joined; partial results are still merged (best-effort, fail-closed contract).
  - `TerminateRuntime` goes through the default backend's scanner.
  - **Forwarding requires a scanning default backend.** The ACP scanner tracks only ACP-hosted sessions, so behind a scannerless default (`hybrid`, `herdr`, `t3bridge`, `exec`, `k8s`) it would report every live default-hosted runtime carrying `GC_SESSION_ID` as an untracked orphan. With a scannerless default, `auto` finds nothing and refuses to terminate.
- **`internal/runtime/process_table_scanner.go`** (new): `runtime.ConditionalProcessTableScanner` + `runtime.AsProcessTableScanner`. `auto` reports `CanScanProcessTable() == false` behind a scannerless default, and the three scanner consumers (`killExistingOrphans`, `sweepProcessTableOrphans`, drain-ack escalation) use the helper instead of a bare type assertion (one-line changes). So cities with a scannerless default see exactly the pre-PR capability, and drain-ack there still records `no_process_table` (not `nothing_attributable`).
- **Mixed-city fix (a reviewer-visible behavior change):** in cities with a scanning default (tmux, subprocess) that also route sessions to ACP, three process-table consumers become active that were previously off:
  1. the pre-start `Manager.killExistingOrphans` sweep;
  2. the per-tick `sweepProcessTableOrphans` (`FindRuntimesBySessionID("")` every controller tick), which kills untracked roots whose session bead is closed or absent. In pure-ACP cities it now also covers ACP roots;
  3. the drain-ack escalation, which now force-terminates tmux seats in mixed cities instead of recording `no_process_table`. For an ACP seat whose runtime survived its stop, the connection is still alive, so it records `nothing_attributable`.

**Inherited-`GC_SESSION_ID` processes.** A root that only inherited `GC_SESSION_ID` (a daemon started from inside the agent) is tracked exactly as long as its session is, then it is eligible for reaping, as with tmux and subprocess. City infrastructure is handled by main, which this branch now includes: managed Dolt no longer inherits session identity (#6316, fixed by 0781b10462), and `killExistingOrphans` and `sweepProcessTableOrphans` refuse `proctable.IsCityInfrastructureRoot` roots (2332772d2d). Those fences sit in the consumers, so they cover roots surfaced by the ACP and `auto` scanners too.

**Residual windows** (documented on `FindRuntimesBySessionID`; all fail toward keeping a process alive except the first): a foreign owner's agent between process start and socket bind reads untracked for that moment, so callers still reap only sessions they have independently established are not running; a replacement session bound to the same socket path makes the previous incarnation's escaped children read as tracked.

**Relation to the linked issues:**
- #5218 (ACP runtimes leak on drain-ack) is **not** addressed here: a leaked runtime whose owner connection is still alive is tracked, not orphaned. This PR only reaps ACP runtimes whose owner or agent is gone.
- #6172 (`KillByPID` has no infrastructure check): ACP `TerminateRuntime` is another caller of `proctable.KillByPID`. It relies on the scanner's infrastructure exclu [truncated]

PR title: fix(runtime): merge auto and hybrid session-event streams and skip nested composites without one

PR description:
## Summary

`auto` and `hybrid` `SubscribeSessionEvents` return only the first event-capable backend's stream. Two problems follow:

1. When both backends publish session events (for example herdr as the default backend plus ACP agents, once the ACP provider publishes events in #6601), the second backend's session deaths never reach the `cmd/gc` session-event pump.
2. A composite always has a `SubscribeSessionEvents` method, so a nested composite with no event-capable backend counts as an implementer. With `[session] provider = "hybrid"` plus ACP agents, production builds `auto(hybrid(tmux, k8s), acp)` (`cmd/gc/providers.go`). `auto` then asks hybrid, gets hybrid's "neither local nor remote backend implements SubscribeSessionEvents" error, and fails the whole subscribe, although the ACP backend has a working stream.

**Change** (new file `internal/runtime/session_events_merge.go`; `auto.go` and `hybrid.go` each call it)
- `runtime.SubscribeSessionEventSources(ctx, a, b)` subscribes to both backends of a composite:
  - a backend returning the new `runtime.ErrNoSessionEventSource` sentinel (a nested composite without a stream) is treated like a backend that does not implement the interface: skipped, and nothing is logged
  - any other subscribe error fails the whole subscribe, with the backend named, so no caller is told a backend is covered while its events are missing (the same policy as #6368, which keeps its `EventCapableRoute` truthful)
  - no stream: an error wrapping `ErrNoSessionEventSource`, so an enclosing composite skips it in turn
  - one stream: returned unchanged, as before
  - two streams: merged by `runtime.MergeSessionEvents`
- `runtime.MergeSessionEvents(ctx, a, b)` closes only when `ctx` ends or both inputs have closed. One input going quiet or closing early does not close it. Each input already honors the `SessionEventProvider` contract (opening `resync`, loss coalesced into `resync`), so the merged stream does too.

### Relationship to #6368 (merge order)

#6368 (@sjarmak, queued-nudge delivery on `agent_idle`) rewrites the same two methods and adds `runtime.MergeSessionEvents(ctx, a, b)`. This PR credits and adopts that design: the same helper name, signature and close semantics, and the same "fail the subscribe on a backend error" policy. What this PR adds on top is the `ErrNoSessionEventSource` sentinel, so nested composites (`auto(hybrid(...), acp)`) are handled.

- **Preferred order: #6368 first, then this PR.** This PR then rebases to the sentinel delta: drop the duplicate `MergeSessionEvents`, keep `SubscribeSessionEventSources` (or fold the sentinel check into #6368's method bodies).
- If this PR lands first, #6368 conflicts textually in `auto.go`/`hybrid.go` and would define `MergeSessionEvents` twice (it adds it to `session_events.go`; this PR adds it to `session_events_merge.go`), so it would drop its copy on rebase.

This PR does not add `EventCapableRoute`; that stays with #6368.

**Stack:** independent of the ACP stack; based on `main`. It becomes useful for ACP once #6601 (ACP session events) lands, but neither depends on the other. Related ACP stack: #6541 then #6599 then #6601.

PR title: fix(env): passthroughEnv honors GC_SUPERVISOR_ENV for session forwarding

PR description:
There doesn't seem to be a way, currently, to allow agents access to custom env vars other than setting them in the city.toml workspace vars which is not optimal. Ideally we should be able to specify which env vars from the host are available to the agents. This fix aims to allow that without creating a new mechanism but using the existing `GC_SUPERVISOR_ENV` env var.

## Summary

Two independent allowlists gated whether a custom (non-`GC_`-prefixed) environment variable ever reached a spawned agent session:

- `GC_SUPERVISOR_ENV` controls what `supervisorServiceExtraEnv` persists into the generated systemd/launchd service file (`cmd_supervisor_lifecycle.go`).
- `passthroughEnv` (`cmd_start.go`) controls what actually gets forwarded into each spawned agent session's environment — but its sweep only ever forwarded `GC_`-prefixed keys, and never consulted `GC_SUPERVISOR_ENV`.

A variable could be fully opted into `GC_SUPERVISOR_ENV`, survive a supervisor restart, and sit in the daemon's own `os.Environ()` — and still silently never reach an agent session, because the two allowlists never talked to each other. There's no error at either stage; the variable just isn't there when the agent looks for it.

## Change

`passthroughEnv` now also forwards any variable named in `GC_SUPERVISOR_ENV`, reusing the existing `supervisorServiceExplicitEnvKeys` parser so the accepted syntax (comma or space separated) is identical to the persistence side. One opt-in list now governs both "survives a supervisor restart" and "reaches every agent session," instead of two allowlists that have to be kept in sync by hand.

`controllerOnlyEnvKeys` is still checked unconditionally, before either the `GC_` prefix check or the new explicit-opt-in check — an operator cannot use `GC_SUPERVISOR_ENV` to un-pin the controller token or other controller-only secrets. Covered by `TestPassthroughEnvSupervisorEnvOptInCannotUnpinControllerToken`.

## Caveat (documented in troubleshooting.md)

`GC_SUPERVISOR_ENV` itself must be present in the supervisor daemon's own process environment for this to take effect after a restart — it isn't automatically persisted into the generated service file the way `PATH`/`GC_HOME` are. ## 1. bd 1.3.1 nested config keys (ga-p9iuv.40)

**Problem.** bd 1.3.1 (beads #6578) writes `bd config set dolt.host|dolt.port|dolt.mode|...` in nested form (`dolt:` / `    host: ...`), and it moves an existing flat key into that form. gc's readers only understood the flat spelling. After an operator or bd touched the endpoint, gc read no host or port, so every repair path on a direct or external scope failed closed. bd 1.3.0 already nests a key that has no flat line, so some v1.3.0 scopes are affected too.

**Root cause.** `internal/beads/contract/files.go` `configStringValue` → `findValue` does an exact top-level key match. The line-scan fallback `scanConfigLineValueFromData` does the same. The same flat-only assumption appears in:
- `gc-beads-bd.sh` `scope_is_proxied` (sed on `dolt.mode`) and `provider_owned_scope_is_local` (greps on `gc.endpoint_origin`, `dolt.auto-start` and `dolt.(host|port|socket)`)
- the dolt pack's health zombie scan (`grep '^dolt\.port:'`, which can flag a rig-local server as a zombie)
- `schemas/wisps-composite-index/common.sh` `config_value`
- the dashboard sampler (`yaml:"dolt.mode"`)

**Fix.**
- `findConfigValue` checks the flat key first and then the nested path, which is the same precedence bd uses (viper tries the longest prefix first, and bd's YAML reader checks flat before nested). It is used by every contract reader and by the line-scan fallback.
- `EnsureCanonicalConfig` and its malformed-YAML fallback now clear the nested spelling of every dotted key they write or delete, so the file ends up with exactly one value per key. Before this, a managed-city canonicalize deleted only the flat `dolt.host`, and bd kept dialing the nested one. `dolt.disable-event-flush` and the F9 `dolt.shared-server` pin, which gc owns in nested form, are left alone.
- The shell readers share one awk helper, `beads_config_value`, which also checks flat first and then nested. The dashboard sampler also reads `dolt: {mode:}`.
- Checked and unchanged: the F9 shared-server pin reader and writer already handle both spellings, `checks_dolt_local_only` already handles both, and metadata.json is identical between the two bd versions (bd writes no nested keys there).

## 2. Stale "bd refuses proxied backup" text

**Problem.** `internal/doctor/proxied_provider.go:32`, the `proxied-backup-coverage` advisory (`checks_proxied_backup_coverage.go:90-91`) and `engdocs/design/beads-proxied-local-default.md` (~316-324) all say bd refuses backup on proxied scopes. From hotfix/1.3.1 onward (#6582/#6584/#6694) that is false.

**Fix.** `proxied-backup-coverage` now runs `bd backup status --json` in each locally stored proxied scope, using the pinned bd and the same scrubbed store env as the custom-types check, with a 30s bound. The result depends on what bd answers, not on a version string:
- If bd refuses (`proxy.backup.unsupported`, v1.3.0), you get today's advisory unchanged: status OK and "the store is the only copy".
- If bd answers, the check verifies a destination is configured and `last_sync` is within 24h. Otherwise it warns at advisory severity: no destination, never synced, stale, or status unreadable. The fix hint is `gc order run mol-dog-backup` or `bd backup init`/`sync`.

- asks bd only about a scope whose proxy gc's own `proxyendpoint.Inspect` (record plus process table, no dial) shows live, and reports the others as "not checked: store not running";
- is registered only when the bead-store preflight passed;
- skips suspended rigs, the same gating the custom-types check uses;
- runs all scopes under one 45s deadline, at most 4 bd calls at a time.

PR title: fix(test): commit the transient-once budget only against a landed failure (ga-njhh8e)

PR description:
## What

Fixes the recurring `TestRetryManagedPooledWorkerRecoversClaimedAttemptAfterCrash`
missing-retry-attempt flake tracked by **ga-j88sfp**, which has blocked or
escalated four release gates in eight days (09-08, 09-11, 09-13, 09-15), each on
a candidate with no path overlap.

Investigation bead: ga-njhh8e.

## Root cause — the test harness, not the production retry path

`should_fail_transient_once` in `test/agents/graph-dispatch.sh` consumed its
one-shot budget **at decision time**: it wrote the marker as a side effect of
deciding to inject.

`close_with_result` deliberately swallows every `bd` error (its own comment says
so, and the rationale is sound: a transient `bd` error would otherwise kill the
worker mid-loop under `set -e`). So when the failing close did not land, the
attempt bead stayed open with the budget already spent. The next pass over that
bead saw the marker, declined to inject, fell through to the normal path, and
closed the attempt `gc.outcome=pass`. `classifyRetryAttempt` then reads a clean
pass, correctly schedules no retry, and the workflow finalizes pass with only
`.attempt.1`.

That is exactly the observed shape in all four sightings: `.attempt.1` present,
`.attempt.2` absent, workflow pass.

**The production side is correct throughout.** Given an attempt closed pass with
no failure metadata, `internal/dispatch/retry.go:416` declining to retry is the
right behavior. Real retries are not being lost. The harness was mislabeling a
failed attempt as a passing one. The `transient-once` pattern has no production
analogue — it exists only under `test/`.

## Fix

Split the decision from the commit:

- `should_fail_transient_once` is now a pure predicate with no side effect.
- `commit_transient_once` writes the marker, and the main loop calls it only
  after reading back `status=closed outcome=fail`.

A dropped close now leaves the budget owed so the next pass re-injects; a landed
close still spends it exactly once.

## Diagnostics

The missing-attempt assertion now dumps workflow state. A real gate failure
previously carried only the step list — the entire `ga-3r36gw` recovery log is
592 bytes, one assertion line, no worker trace. That ambiguity (a lost injection
and a controller that declined to retry look identical) is why this stayed
unrooted across four sightings. The new `transient-once-uncommitted` trace line
names a dropped close directly.

## Evidence

- Regression test `TestGraphDispatchTransientOnceBudgetSurvivesLostClose`
  extracts the real shell functions and pins all three properties: budget
  survives a close that never landed, budget is spent once the close lands,
  unselected refs are never injected.
- Verified RED against the pre-fix source and GREEN after: two decisions with no
  landed close leave the injection owed under the fix, and lose it before it.
- Alternative hypothesis disproved: "the attempt-1 outcome is recorded pass
  before the transient injection takes effect" is structurally impossible —
  `should_fail_transient_once` is consulted *before* any pass-close path in the
  same loop iteration and `continue`s past it. The only route to `.attempt.1`
  closing pass is a previously-consumed marker.

## Scope

Covers **ga-j88sfp** only. Two other open trackers on the same test are distinct
conditions and are explicitly **not** addressed here:

- **ga-oc46fi** — `.attempt.2` did materialize; the trace lacked the success
  entry. Different phase.
- **ga-tot0gw** — `gc init` colliding with an incompatible active supervisor.
  Environmental.

## Census

The new test executes the real shell functions through one `bash` subprocess —
the same idiom the sibling `TestGraphDispatchHookFallbackForNamedWorker` already
uses in this file — so the all-source subprocess census grows by one call (file
count unchanged; the file already spawns). Pinned in the three places the
manifest header requires to move together: the Go `bootstrapPolicy`,
`test-resources.toml`, and the generated `TESTING.md` row.

## Testing

- `TestGraphDispatchTransientOnceBudgetSurvivesLostClose` passes (3 subtests).
- Pre-existing `TestGraphDispatchHookFallbackForNamedWorker` still passes.
- `go vet -tags integration ./test/integration/` clean.
- `shellcheck -S warning` on the script reports only a pre-existing SC2034 at
  line 453, outside this diff.
- Full pre-push suite green.

**Not verified locally:** the live integration test cannot run in this
environment — it fails at `bd init` on the pending Dolt schema migration
(ga-3jtbpm). Confirmed environmental by running it at clean `origin/main` in a
scratch worktree: identical failure, same point. CI exercises it properly.

PR title: fix(runtime): guard standalone store handles against reload races

PR description:
## Summary

A city running without controller state (API disabled) keeps its own city and rig bead store handles, and every config reload reopens them. The reload swapped those handles with no synchronization while the route-recovery backstop, completions and detached-orphan lanes read them on their own goroutines. That is a data race: a lane can read a torn/stale handle, or see a freshly opened store before its fields are visible (the race detector flags `FileStore` and `beadPolicyStore` internals written by the open and read by the lane's `List`).

## Root cause

`reloadConfigTraced` (and `run()` at startup) assigned `cr.standaloneCityStore` / `cr.standaloneRigStores` directly, while `cityBeadStore()` / `rigBeadStores()` read them unlocked from background lanes (`route_recovery.go` `routeRecoveryPlan` / `routeRecoveryRigStores`).

## Fix

- New `setStandaloneStores` writes both handles under `serviceStateMu`; `cityBeadStore` / `rigBeadStores` read them under its read lock when there is no controller state.
- Stores are opened before the lock is taken, so readers never wait on an open.
- Deadlock check: no path that already holds `serviceStateMu` (`publishRuntimeConfig`, `serviceConfigSnapshot`, the convergence snapshots, `serviceRuntime` accessors) calls either accessor, so no lock nesting is added. The rig map is replaced whole, never mutated in place.

## Tests

- `TestRouteRecoveryBackstopConcurrentWithStandaloneStoreReload` runs route-recovery backstop passes back to back across a real config reload of a standalone runtime. Under `-race` it fails on main (8/8 fresh processes) and passes with the fix. No sleeps or listeners, so the test-resource ledger is unchanged.

PR title: refactor(controller): carry reconcile keys on every controller wake-up

PR description:
## What

Reconciler v2, slice P1.2: every controller wake-up now carries a reconcile key, from the trigger all the way to the controller.

- New `internal/reconcilekey` package. A `Key` is one of three kinds: allocator, session (by bead ID, runtime name, or both) or control_dispatch. Keys that are empty or malformed normalize to allocator.
- `api.State.Poke()` is replaced by `Enqueue(keys...)`. Every API trigger now names what it concerns: session create, named-session materialize (plus the retired rows it replaces), permission-mode change, sling notifier.
- On the CLI side, `pokeController` call sites that concern a session now go through `enqueueController(cityPath, key)` (session new/suspend/reset/kill/wake/pin, drain, handoff, nudge, sling). `wireControllerWakeSignals` wires `controllerState` to both wake channels, for the standalone controller and for the supervisor's per-city start.

## Why: no behavior change under the legacy reconciler

`legacyEnqueue` maps every key onto the same wake it replaces. Allocator and session keys send one non-blocking send on `pokeCh`, and they coalesce exactly like `Poke()` did. The control-dispatch key sends one send on `controlDispatcherCh`. Keyed wakes therefore still produce a `"poke"` tick, so the live session-snapshot read from #6763 still runs. The keys exist so that a keyed reconciler can route on them later.

## Socket protocol compatibility (both directions)

- **New controller, old client:** the bare `poke` still works and means allocator. `poke:<json key>` is accepted, and an empty or malformed payload degrades to allocator.
- **New client, old controller:** a session key goes out as `poke:<json>`. If the controller closes the connection without replying (how an old controller treats an unknown verb) or replies with anything other than `ok`, the client retries once with plain `poke`. It does not retry when the controller is unavailable or the read times out, so a hung controller costs one timeout, not two. Allocator and control-dispatch keys keep the legacy `poke` / `control-dispatcher` verbs. The supervisor fallback is the same as `pokeController`'s.

## The one behavior fix (OQ-6)

The API sling notifier's `PokeControlDispatch` used to call the generic poke, so workflow launches through the API never ran the targeted control-dispatcher reconcile. It now enqueues the control-dispatch key, the same as the CLI's `control-dispatcher` socket command.

## Tests

- Table tests for key normalize, encode and decode, and for `legacyEnqueue` mapping and coalescing.
- Controller socket `poke` / `poke:<key>` handling.
- Keyed poke against key-aware, legacy, hung and missing controllers, plus the supervisor fallback.
- `pokeControllerForRestart` never falls back to the supervisor.
- Wake-signal wiring for both the standalone and the supervisor controller paths.
- A key assertion for each API trigger (the async ones were run with `-race -count=10`).
- The tests stay within the no-grow test resource ledger (`internal/testpolicy/resourcecensus` passes).

PR description:
## Why
Every `bazel test` run on main starts with ~90 of 182 tests failing to build with `Lost inputs no longer available remotely: external/rules_go+/stdlib_/pkg/linux_amd64/internal/runtime/cgobench.a`, then Bazel prints `Found transient remote cache error, retrying the build...` and the second pass succeeds. The restored output base (`actions/cache`, key = hash of `MODULE.bazel.lock`) is never re-saved: a primary-key hit skips the save. Its local action cache still records stdlib outputs that exist only in the old farm's CAS. rbe-west has never had that blob (a direct ByteStream read returns NOT_FOUND), so any Go change that needs it as an input fails, and Bazel restarts the build.

- `bazel-v2-` prefix drops the frozen entry.
- UTC-day suffix re-saves the output base daily, so its records track the current CAS.
- `restore-keys` fall back to the latest entry for the same lockfile, then any `v2` entry, so runs stay warm.

Expect the first run after merge to be cold-ish (fresh output base, remote cache still warm). actionlint and `go test ./scripts/...` pass locally.

v1.5.0 cities default to bd-owned proxied Dolt (#6273). The core `reaper` and `jsonl-export` orders and the dolt pack's `mol-dog-backup` spoke raw SQL / the `dolt` CLI to a gc-resolved Dolt port and enumerated `SHOW DATABASES` on one server. PR title: fix(session): roll back pending creates through the fenced atomic close

PR description:
## Summary

The controller rolls back a failed or abandoned pending create through `rollbackPendingCreateClears` (`cmd/gc/session_lifecycle_parallel.go`). `rollbackPendingCreate`, `rollbackPendingCreateClearingClaim` and `rollbackPendingCreateMarkingTerminal` all share it. It wrote the pre-close clears, the failed-create terminal patch, the Close and the explicit `session_name` clear in one `store.Tx`.

That Tx is atomic on native Dolt and SQLite. On FileStore, and on a CachingStore over it, it runs as **separate writes**. A wake stamping `state=awake` between the failed-create metadata and the Close left the row `status=closed state=awake`, and the reconciler and `gc session list` read that as a live session. This is the last controller path in the closed-but-awake class after #6745, #6747 and #6784. #6784 deliberately left it for a separate change because of its name-release ordering.

The same Tx was also **unconditional** after the rollback fence's read. So a writer from another process that landed in the window got closed over:
- a new incarnation;
- a completed start (`state=active`, claim cleared);
- a `gc session kill` fence (#6749).

On a cached front door, the fence could also approve a stale cached row and then close a newer incarnation. The new tests reproduce all of these on main.

## Root cause

`rollbackPendingCreateClears` never consulted `beads.AtomicConditionalCloser`. FileStore, SQLite, native Dolt and a CachingStore over any of them provide it.

## Fix

New `session.Store.RollbackPendingCreateAtomically`:

- **Fenced close.** It holds the same per-session mutation lock as `WithPendingCreateRollback`, start completion and incarnation allocation, and reads the row once.
  - That read must pass `PendingCreateLease.CanRollback`, the same check as today. Its revision fences one `CloseWithMetadataIfMatch` carrying the pre-close clears plus the failed-create patch. The failed-create keys overlay the pre-close ones, the same result as the Tx's write order.
  - It shares `closeAtomically` with `Close` and `CloseWithTerminalPatch`.
  - `CloseWithTerminalPatch` itself isn't enough here. It re-reads on its own and only checks the kill fence, so the rollback's identity and claim fence would not hold across that re-read or a lost fence.
- **Lost fence.** It re-reads and closes only if the re-read row still passes `CanRollback`. It makes at most 3 attempts and never degrades to a split write. A kill fence always fails `CanRollback`, because `KillPendingPatch` clears the claim, so the rollback yields to it.
- **Name-release ordering is kept.** The `session_name` clear is a separate write, made only after the close succeeded and only while the row still reads closed.
  - Where the store resolves a conditional writer, that write is fenced on the revision it re-read.
  - A row reopened in between keeps its name, and the mirrored batch then leaves out the clear.
  - If the close lands but the name clear fails, the existing error branch runs retired-session cleanup, as it does for a split Tx today.
- **Stores without the capability** keep the historical Tx verbatim. That covers BdStore, exec, plain MemStore and a legacy sqlite layout, and also a store that refuses the atomic close at call time (conditional writes disabled). The refusal writes nothing.
- **Unchanged:**
  - #6744's liveness gates, which run before the rollback;
  - the three-outcome `rollbackPendingCreateConfirmed`;
  - the in-flight lease and claim ordering on the Tx arm.

## Tests

`cmd/gc/session_rollback_pending_create_atomic_test.go` reuses #6784's race harness. It covers AtomicCloseMemStore, FileStore, SQLiteStore, CachingStore over FileStore, and plain MemStore as the fallback.

- `TestRollbackPendingCreateKeepsAConcurrentWakeOutOfTheClosedRow` is the regression. It runs all three rollback helpers on every backend.
  - **On main it fails:** `state="awake"` on a closed row on every split-Tx store, and every capable store takes the Tx.
  - With the fix it passes: one lost fence, one retry, no Tx. MemStore pins the unchanged Tx.
- `TestRollbackPendingCreateReleasesTheNameOnlyAfterTheClose`: the write order is `close,clear-session_name`. The atomic close never carries `session_name`, and right after the close the row is closed and still named.
- `TestRollbackPendingCreateKeepsTheNameWhenTheCloseFails`: a writer wins every fence. The row stays open with its name, claim and `last_woke_at`, and the confirmed outcome is `pendingCreateRollbackFailed`.
- `TestRollbackPendingCreateLeavesAReopenedRowItsName`: the unfenced post-close branch.
- `TestRollbackPendingCreateFencesHoldOnTheAtomicClose` lands a new incarnation, a completed start, or a kill fence in the window. The row is left alone, and the outcome is `pendingCreateRollbackSuperseded`. **On main it fails:** all three get closed over.
- `TestRollbackPendingCreateRefusesAStaleObservationBeforeWriting`. **On main it fails** on the cache: the stale cached row is closed.
- `TestRollbackPendingCreateFallsBackToTheTxWhenTheCloseIsRefused`: FileStore with conditional writes disabled.
- `TestRollbackPendingCreateUnderRealConcurrentWritersNeverRestsClosedAwake` runs six real rollbacks and a fenced awake writer, with a turn handshake before each terminal write (the rollback hands the writer one stamp attempt) to open the window deterministically.
  - **On main:** FileStore and the cache failed in 10 of 10 runs, AtomicCloseMemStore in 7 of 10.
  - With the fix it passes `-race -count=10`.

  - a lost fence re-reads and retries without undoing the other write;
  - a reopen that lands between the re-read and the write keeps the name;
  - the unsupported signal writes nothing.

records.title: fix(tmux): stop steady invalidation from starving StateCache into all-absent
records.request:
PR title: fix(tmux): stop steady invalidation from starving StateCache into all-absent

PR description:
## Summary

`StateCache` could report **every** tmux session as absent while tmux showed them all running. `refresh()` threw away any successful fetch that an `Invalidate`/`EvictSession` had superseded mid-flight, and it did not advance `fetchedAt`. On a busy city an invalidation (a session start, relaunch, or stop) can land during every 1–3s fetch. When that happens nothing new is ever published. Once the 30s `staleTTL` passes, `currentState` returns an empty snapshot and `IsRunning` returns false for every session. That false "absent" feeds reconciler decisions that drain, restart, or reap healthy sessions.

Reproduced on main with a fetcher that invalidates during every fetch: all ~50 fetches listed the session as running, and `IsRunning` still returned false once `staleTTL` elapsed.

## Root cause

The generation check was added to stop an in-flight fetch from undoing `Stop`'s `EvictSession`. It did that by discarding the whole observation, so it also discarded the evidence that the server is up. Steady invalidation turns "discard this one" into "never publish again".

## Fix

- **Publish a superseded fetch, with evicted sessions filtered out.** `EvictSession` records the generation its eviction produced. Any session evicted after the fetch began is removed before publishing, so a session that `Stop` killed mid-fetch is not resurrected by an older fetch that still listed it. The cache stays **dirty** so the next read refreshes again. `fetchedAt` advances because the server really was observed.
- **Never publish an older observation over a newer one.** A dirty read forgets the in-flight singleflight, so two fetches can overlap. The cache records the start generation of the published snapshot and discards a fetch that started before it.
- **The unprimed no-server path follows the same rules.** It primes an empty snapshot, records its start generation, and stays dirty if an invalidation landed mid-fetch instead of clearing it.

Invariants kept: copy-on-write for the published map (the filter clones before deleting, as #6735 requires). Each read still does at most one fetch. Eviction semantics are unchanged. Eviction records at or below the published generation are pruned on publish, so the map stays bounded.

## Tests

New file `internal/runtime/tmux/state_cache_superseded_refresh_test.go` (registered in `BUILD.bazel` and `scripts/runtime-tmux-tests.manifest`, counts updated):

- `TestStateCache_SteadyInvalidationDoesNotStarveToFalseAbsent`: every fetch is superseded and the last publish is aged past `staleTTL` before each read (no sleeps). Every read keeps reporting the session running, with exactly one fetch per read, and the cache stays dirty. **Fails on main.**
- `TestStateCache_SupersededRefreshKeepsSessionEvictedMidFetch`: a session evicted during an in-flight fetch stays absent. The rest of that fetch is published, `fetchedAt` advances, dirty holds, the fetcher's map is not mutated, and the follow-up refresh settles the cache and prunes eviction records. **Fails on main** (`fetchedAt` not advanced).
- `TestStateCache_SupersededRefreshDoesNotOverwriteNewerPublish`: an older superseded fetch landing after a newer publish is discarded. Guards the overlap case; it fails if the publish-order check is removed.
- `TestStateCache_UnprimedNoServerStaysDirtyWhenSupersededMidFetch`: the empty prime does not clear an invalidation that landed mid-fetch. **Fails on main.**

I also ran mutation checks: removing the eviction filter, the clone, or the keep-dirty rule each fails at least one of these tests. The existing `state_cache` tests pass unchanged, including `TestStateCache_DiscardRefreshAfterEvictSession` and the #6735 race tests. `go test -race ./internal/runtime/tmux/` is clean.

records.request:
PR title: fix(api): run pack import add/remove as a config transaction the reload honors

PR description:
## Summary

The HTTP pack import endpoints (`POST /v0/city/{cityName}/packs` and `DELETE /v0/city/{cityName}/packs/{name}`) write several config files. The controller's runtime config reload could read them in the middle of that write and publish a split pack set. A failed import could also leave a half-written pack set on disk for the next reload to publish.

## Root cause

`importsvc` add/remove syncs the lock graph, saves `pack.toml` (or `city.toml`), and then writes `packs.lock`. The handlers ran this through `controllerState.SerializeConfigWrite`, which only took the `configedit.Editor` lock. The runtime reload never takes that lock. As a result:

- a reload between those writes read a split generation: a new `[imports]` entry with the old lockfile, or the reverse;
- when a later step failed (for example the `packs.lock` write), the files already written stayed on disk;
- a successful write was never published to the controller state, unlike every other API config mutation (`mutateAndPoke`).

## Fix

`SerializeConfigWrite` becomes a real per-city config transaction:

- It holds a new config transaction fence, then the Editor lock.
- It snapshots `pack.toml`, `packs.lock` and `city.toml`, and restores them if the callback fails.
- It publishes the result through `mutateAndPoke`: refresh, pending mark, poke, and rollback if the new generation does not load. The rollback snapshot now also covers `pack.toml` and `packs.lock`.

Rig provisioning, the other multi-file writer, runs under the same fence.

The runtime reload `TryLock`s the fence around its candidate load. If a transaction is in flight, the reload defers and leaves itself pending instead of reading a half-written generation. It never blocks the reconciler behind a slow git import, and it does not poke, so it cannot spin; the transaction pokes when it publishes.

Snapshot restore now skips files whose bytes are unchanged, so a rejected request (for example 409 import-exists) does not churn mtimes or wake the config watcher.

**No HTTP API, OpenAPI or genclient change.** The Go seam keeps its signature and the handlers are untouched. The enterprise version added a context-aware seam with new 408/501/504 responses; I dropped that because it isn't needed for the fix.

## Tests

New file `cmd/gc/api_state_pack_transaction_test.go`:

- `TestControllerStatePackConfigWriteRollsBackPartialWriteOnError`
- `TestControllerStatePackConfigWriteRollsBackPackFilesWhenRefreshFails`
- `TestControllerStatePackConfigWritePublishesGeneration`
- `TestCityRuntimeReloadDefersWhilePackConfigWriteInFlight`: a reload attempted mid-transaction defers, leaves the loop on its generation with a retry pending, and the next reload applies the finished generation.

All four fail on `origin/main` and pass with the fix, including under `-race`. `internal/api` passes, as does the `Reload|CityRuntime|ControllerState|Rig|Pack|Import|Mutat|Formula` subset of `cmd/gc`.

The loop and the API then disagreed until some unrelated config change triggered another reload. On a provider change the loop also announced a provider swap the controller never adopted.

## Root cause

`CityRuntime.reloadConfigTraced` did three things in this order:

1. assigned the candidate config, session provider and drain ops to the loop (`cr.cfg`, `cr.sp`, `cr.dops`), and later advanced `cr.configRev`;
2. only then called `controllerState.updateFromRuntime`;
3. relied on `updateFromRuntime`, which silently drops a candidate that a newer config superseded while the reload was preparing it. That newer config can be an API mutation (pending revision), an on-disk edit, or a failure to load the current revision.

`updateFromRuntime` returned nothing, so the loop could not tell it had been rejected. The reload reported "Config reloaded", and the provider-swap path advanced `lastProviderName` and emitted `provider.swapped`. Separately, the same-revision "bead store metadata changed" path called `cs.update` unconditionally, so it could overwrite a newer pending API mutation with an older config.

## Fix

- `updateFromRuntime` now reports whether it accepted the candidate. `runtimeUpdateWouldBeAccepted` is its read-only half.
- The reload publishes through `publishRuntimeConfig`, which asks the controller state first and advances the loop only if it accepts.
- On rejection the reload:
  - keeps the current generation (config, provider, drain ops, `configRev`, order dispatcher);
  - returns a failed "superseded …; retry scheduled" reply;
  - leaves the reload dirty for the next tick. It does not poke: whoever superseded the candidate (the config watcher or the API mutation) already pokes, and a rejection that repeats on the same revision would otherwise spin reconciliation ticks.
- A provider-changing reload checks acceptance before stopping sessions for the swap, since that step cannot be undone. It announces the swap and advances `lastProviderName` only after publication succeeds.
- The outgoing order dispatcher is still drained before publication. It joins the retired list only when it is actually replaced.
- The same-revision metadata path goes through the same acceptance check.

## Tests

New file `cmd/gc/city_runtime_config_publication_test.go`:

- `TestCityRuntimeReloadRejectsRevisionSupersededDuringPreparation`: an on-disk edit lands mid-reload.
- `TestCityRuntimeReloadSupersededByAPIMutationConvergesOnRetry`: an API `CreateAgent` lands mid-reload. The loop keeps its generation, and the retry converges both snapshots on the mutation.
- `TestCityRuntimeProviderReloadSupersededDuringCensusDoesNotPublishSwap`
- `TestCityRuntimeProviderReloadAlreadySupersededSkipsProviderEffects`: sessions are never listed or stopped for a stale provider swap.
- Unit tests for `publishRuntimeConfig` and the level-triggered, no-poke retry.
- The existing `updateFromRuntime` tests now assert the accept/reject result.

The four reload-level tests fail on `origin/main` (the reload reports `applied`) and pass with the fix. They also pass under `-race`. The broader `Reload|CityRuntime|ControllerState|Order|Provider|Mutat` subset of `cmd/gc` passes.

This also carries the enterprise test cleanup 01ed42ab7d. It makes the one-second shutdown-timeout config helper parameter-free, which the new call site needs to stay clean under `unparam`.

records.request:
PR title: fix(start): take the controller lock before starting the bead-store provider

PR description:
## Summary

`gc start --foreground` started the bead-store provider before it tried the controller lock. It also ran the provider's init, health and warm-up ops before that point, and only took the lock inside `runController`. So a foreground start that lost the lock had already run provider ops against a provider it did not own. That was either a live controller's provider, or one that `gc stop` was retiring while it held the lock (#6742). The start then exited with `controller already running` and left behind whatever it had started or restarted. That can include a provider still running after `gc stop` reported the city stopped.

This is the gap noted while landing #6742. `gc stop` now holds the lock through provider shutdown, but a racing start could still restart the provider underneath that stop.

## Root cause

The standalone start did its whole preparation, provider start included, first, and only then tried the controller lock. The lock is the only thing that says who owns the city.

## Fix

- `doStartStandalone` takes the controller lock right after the city scaffold, before any provider op. It holds the lock through the controller run (`defer`, so every exit path releases it) and passes it to `runController`.
- `runController` takes a new `heldLock` argument. When the caller already holds the lock, `runController` uses it and leaves the release to the caller. When `heldLock` is nil, it acquires the lock itself as before. Either way the lock is still released last, after the socket and the rest of shutdown.
- A dry run never becomes the controller, so it previews without the lock.
- The warm-up doctor scan no longer probes the flock while the start holds it, because the probe would only find the start's own lock.

Provider ops already run under the held lock today: the running controller's bead-store health and recovery restart the provider while it holds the lock. The lock descriptor is close-on-exec, so the provider's long-lived server does not inherit it. A test checks this.

**Not changed: the supervisor-hosted start.** It takes the lock only after city preparation. Taking it before `startBeadsLifecycle` would mean holding the flock with no controller socket for the whole bead-store start, which can take minutes. `ensureNoStandaloneController` reads "lock held, no socket" as a controller of unknown hosting. So `gc start` or `gc register` would then fail against any city the supervisor is still booting, including the normal case of `gc start` right after it restarts a drifted supervisor. Under the supervisor, the only way to race a stop is an explicit concurrent `gc start` or `gc register`. That start loses the lock, and `retrySupervisorCityStartAfterControllerLock` retries it once the stop releases the lock. It re-runs the bead-store start, so the city ends up running, which is what the later command asked for.

## Tests

`cmd/gc/cmd_start_controller_lock_test.go` (registered in `BUILD.bazel`). The provider is an exec script that logs each op and whether the controller lock was held when it ran.

- `TestStartForegroundLeavesBeadsProviderAloneWhileControllerLockHeld`: while another owner holds the controller lock, `gc start --foreground` exits 1 with the lock refusal and runs no provider ops. On main it ran `start`, `init`, `health` and `list-by-label` against the provider before failing on the lock.
- `TestStartForegroundStartsBeadsProviderUnderControllerLock`: the provider's first op, `start`, runs with the controller lock held. When the start fails, the lock is free again, even though the provider left a long-lived child running. On main, `start` ran with the lock free.

Both tests fail on origin/main (checked against a `git archive` copy of main) and pass with the fix. They also pass under `-race` at `-count=5`. The start, stop, controller, reload, register and warm-up tests in `./cmd/gc` pass, and `make lint-changed` is clean.

PR title: fix(pool): reserve min_active_sessions floors before new demand

PR description:
## Summary

`min_active_sessions` is meant to be a floor: the number of sessions a pool keeps running whatever the demand. It was not one. `applyNestedCaps` accepted every demand request first, spending the workspace counter, and only then walked `cfg.Agents` to add floor requests, stopping at the first rejection. Under load, demand used up the workspace ceiling and floors got nothing. Among floors, the agent earlier in config order won.

On a workspace capped at 13 sessions, a pool with `min_active_sessions = 4` ran one session for over an hour while a `min = 0` pool held three.

This change reserves floor capacity before new demand competes for the caps:

- Existing, in-flight (creating) and post-create protected sessions are accepted first. A floor never evicts a live or starting session of another pool.
- Floors are then reserved against the remaining workspace, rig and agent headroom, in lexical template order when they cannot all fit. The rejected floor is named in the trace.
- New demand competes only for what is left. A template below its own floor spends its own reservation first, so its demand is not double counted.

It also fixes a rig cap that never applied. `newNestedCapLimits` keyed `rigMax` by rig name but looked it up by `agent.Dir`, so any path-shaped `Dir` fell back to "no cap". The lookup now resolves the rig with `agentRigScopeName`, as the rest of the CLI does. An agent whose rig does not resolve gets no new floor or demand sessions, but keeps its existing and in-flight sessions.

## Test plan

- [x] `pool_desired_state_floor_test.go`: 15 new tests covering floor reservation in both config orders, overcommitted floors, existing, in-flight and protected sessions of another pool surviving a competing floor (including a rig-capped floor), the path-shaped `Dir` rig cap, and unresolved-rig refusal.
